pamphlet_excerpts: Focused Attention to Shop Safety: Metal working requires the craftsman to pay close attention to the work at hand and to adhere closely to special safety requirements (p. 16).
Protecting Yourself and Others First: Before diving into the techniques of metal working, learn how to keep yourself and others safe while working with metal (p. 16).
Heat, Acid, and Supervision Rules: When working with metal, acid, and high temperatures, metal workers should be aware of possible hazards, and youths must have adult supervision (p. 16).
Safe and Enjoyable Metalcraft: Following the rules will keep metal working safe and enjoyable (p. 16).

Step 3 - Wear Proper Protective Gear: Paying attention to what you are doing and wearing the proper gear is critical in metal working (p. 16).
Step 4 - Guard Eyes Against Flying Chips: When sheet metal is cut, as mall chip of metal can fly anywhere, possibly into your eye (p. 16).

Include each component's dimensions on your sketch, which need not be to scale. (3) Make two objects out of 24- or 26-gauge sheet metal. requirements.description: After completing the first four requirements, complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Sheet Metal Mechanic/Tinsmith. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and describe the use of the basic sheet metalworking tools. (2) Create a sketch of two objects to make from sheet metal. Include each component's dimensions on your sketch, which need not be to scale. (3) Make two objects out of 24- or 26-gauge sheet metal. Use patterns either provided by your counselor or made by you and approved by your counselor. Construct these objects using a metal that is appropriate to the object's ultimate purpose, and using cutting, bending, edging, and either soldering or brazing. (a) One object also must include at least one riveted component. (b) If you do not make your objects from zinc-plated sheet steel or tin-plated sheet steel, preserve your work from oxidation. (b) Option B, Silversmith. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and describe the use of a silversmith's basic tools. (2) Create a sketch of two objects to make from sheet silver. Include each component's dimensions on your sketch, which need not be to scale. (3) Make two objects out of 18- or 20-gauge sheet copper. Use patterns either provided by your counselor or made by you and approved by your counselor. Both objects must include a soldered joint. If you have prior silversmithing experience, you may substitute sterling silver, nickel silver, or lead-free pewter. (a) At least one object must include a sawed component you have made yourself. (b) At least one object must include a sunken part you have made yourself. (c) Clean and polish your objects. (c) Option C, Founder. Do ALL of the following: (1) Name and describe the use of the basic parts of a two-piece mold. Name at least three different types of molds. (2) Create a sketch of two objects to cast in metal. B. Cold brass melts at room temperature when bent by hand, and hammering turns it into a magnetic ferrous steel
C. Lead and mercury are the only two metals that become harder when hammered along a 45-degree fold line
